# How to Use AI to Turn Your Ideas into Images (Even If You Can't Draw)

> **In short:** Type a description into a free tool like ChatGPT or Microsoft Designer's Image Creator, and you'll get a picture back in seconds. The trick to getting a picture you actually like is a four-part prompt: subject, setting, style, mood.

Picture this. You're planning a kid's birthday party with a "moon adventure" theme. You can see it perfectly in your head — a friendly astronaut bouncing on a fluffy pastel moon — but you can't draw it, and stock photos just don't cut it. This is the kind of moment text-to-image AI was made for.

## Before you start

You'll need:

- A **free account** with the tool you pick. The steps below cover two options: **ChatGPT** (the chatbot at chatgpt.com) and **Microsoft Designer's Image Creator** (free inside the Microsoft Edge browser, or at designer.microsoft.com). Both work on a phone or laptop.
- **No drawing skills, no paid plan, no special software.** Just a web browser.
- A rough idea of what you want to see. The more specific you are, the better the picture.

One honest note before we begin: these tools update their interfaces fairly often, so a button label might shift slightly between the time you read this and the time you click. If something looks different, look for the closest match — the logic is the same.

## Step 1 — Open the tool and start a new image request

Go to **chatgpt.com** (or open Microsoft Edge and head to **designer.microsoft.com**). If you're not already signed in, sign in or create a free account. In ChatGPT, click the **"+"** or **"New chat"** button at the top of the sidebar to start fresh.

You'll see a chat-style text box at the bottom of the screen, the same one you'd use to ask ChatGPT any other question.

💬 Copy and paste this starter prompt:
> *"Draw an image of a friendly astronaut bouncing on a fluffy pastel moon, cartoon style, soft colors."*

You'll know it worked when an image appears in the chat (ChatGPT) or on the design canvas (Image Creator), usually within 5–20 seconds.

## Step 2 — Use the four-part prompt formula

A vague prompt gives a vague picture. So before you ask again, build your description out of four pieces: **subject** (what's in the picture), **setting** (where it is), **style** (photorealistic, cartoon, watercolour, 3D render), and **mood** (cheerful, calm, dramatic, mysterious).

For example, instead of "a cat", try: *"a fluffy ginger cat sleeping on a stack of vintage books, warm afternoon light, soft-focus background, watercolour style."*

💬 Copy and paste this upgraded prompt:
> *"A corgi wearing a tiny chef hat, sitting on a kitchen bench, soft morning light, photorealistic style."*

You'll know it worked when the second image clearly looks like a corgi in a kitchen, rather than a generic blurry dog — that's the four parts doing their job.

## Step 3 — Iterate: tweak the words and try again

Your first image almost certainly won't be exactly right. That's normal — it's a starting point, not the finish line. Read the picture, decide what you want to change, and re-send a tweaked version. Most tools let you click the image and choose **"Edit"**, **"Regenerate"**, or simply type *"make it more …"* in the chat box.

You can change one thing at a time: the color, the lighting, the angle, the style. Each new version usually takes about 10 seconds.

💬 Copy and paste this follow-up prompt:
> *"Same as before, but make the lighting golden-hour sunset and add a few flour dust particles in the air."*

You'll know it worked when the new image is recognizably the same scene but with the changes you asked for baked in.

## Step 4 — Tell the AI what you *don't* want

Most image tools let you list things to avoid. In ChatGPT, just add a negative instruction to your prompt. In Image Creator, look for a small prompt-helper panel or an "exclusions" field on the right side of the canvas — the exact location shifts as Microsoft updates the site.

This step is where beginners save themselves a lot of frustration: most "weird" image results come from unwanted elements the AI added on its own.

💬 Copy and paste this prompt with a negative:
> *"A bowl of fruit on a wooden table, studio lighting, photorealistic. No text, no watermark, no blurry edges."*

You'll know it worked when the image has no stray letters, logos or smudged edges — even if the bowl of fruit is otherwise similar to a version you got without the negatives.

## Step 5 — Save your image and your winning prompt

When you get an image you're happy with, click it to open the full-size view, then look for a **download** icon (usually a downward arrow) or a **"Save"** button. On a phone, you may need to long-press the image and choose **"Save to Photos"**.

Save the prompt that worked too. Paste it into a notes app or a doc labeled "prompts that work". Future-you will thank present-you.

💬 Save this exact wording alongside the image:
> *"Subject + Setting + Style + Mood + 'no text, no watermark' — see corgi/chef prompt, 4 June 2026."*

You'll know it worked when the file is on your device (check your Downloads folder or Photos app) and the prompt text is somewhere you can find again next week.

## Common mistakes

- **Mistake:** Sending a one-word prompt like *"dog"* and expecting a usable picture.
  **Fix:** Always run it through the subject-setting-style-mood formula first. Even adding *"brown labrador, park, sunny afternoon, photorealistic"* lifts the result enormously.

- **Mistake:** Giving up after the first image doesn't match what you imagined.
  **Fix:** Treat the first result as a sketch, not a final. Regenerate two or three times with small wording changes — that's how the tool learns what you want.

- **Mistake:** Asking for images of real, named people or copying a specific living artist's exact style.
  **Fix:** Describe the *kind* of look you want ("watercolour with soft pastel tones") rather than a person's name or a named artist's style. Most tools will refuse or give poor results either way, and it's the ethical route.

- **Mistake:** Asking for the picture to include text like *"Happy Birthday Sarah"* — AI image tools almost always butcher text.
  **Fix:** Generate the picture without text, then add the text yourself in Canva, PowerPoint, or even Notes. Two minutes, and the text is actually readable.

## What this means for you

- **For everyday creative projects:** Make birthday invites, social media graphics, blog headers, or personalized cards without paying a designer.
- **For parents and families:** Generate custom illustrations for kids' stories or school projects — try describing your child's pet or favorite toy.
- **For students:** Need a quick visual for a presentation? A solid prompt gives you something far more interesting than clipart.
- **If you're new to this:** Start with the image generator built into ChatGPT or Microsoft Designer's Image Creator — both are free and forgiving for first-timers.

## Wrap-up

You don't need to be an artist to bring an idea to life. Pick a tool, write a clear prompt using the subject-setting-style-mood formula, and have a play. Save the prompts that work. The first picture is just the starting point — the real fun is in tweaking until you get exactly what you had in your head.

Try this today: open ChatGPT or Image Creator, paste the corgi prompt from Step 2, and see what comes back. Then send Step 3's follow-up to watch it change in front of you.
